widget.name: Aq Nivo
widget.description: Nivo data visualisation — 26 chart types behind one property surface. Choose a chart type, bind a String attribute holding the data as JSON, and configure the chart with static JSON, an attribute holding JSON, or both.

property.caption: Data from
property.description: Where the chart's data comes from. JSON string is the original mode and the only one that supports every chart type: the app builds the payload in the shape Nivo expects and binds it to a String attribute. Data source binds an ordinary Mendix list instead and maps attributes to chart keys below, which is how the rest of Mendix works and is the only mode in which a click can carry the row it fired on to a microflow. Data source cannot express a tree, a graph, a numeric matrix or GeoJSON, so eight chart types are JSON only; the property sheet says which when you pick one.

property.caption: Chart data
property.description: Used when Data from is JSON string. String attribute holding this chart's data as JSON, in the shape the selected chart type expects — see nivo.rocks for the shape per chart type. The attribute must be set to Unlimited length in the domain model: Mendix defaults a String attribute to 200 characters and truncates it silently, which turns valid chart JSON into malformed JSON. The chart then shows a parse error for a reason that is invisible from the page, and reads as a broken data source rather than a too-short column.

property.caption: Chart rows
property.description: Used when Data from is Data source. The list to draw, one row per data point. IMPORTANT: give it rows that are already at chart granularity — a Mendix data source cannot be asked for grouped or aggregated rows, so aggregate in a microflow and return the result. The widget never aggregates and never pages: it draws every row it is given, because charting one page and presenting it as the whole is not slow, it is wrong, and it looks entirely plausible. A chart is aggregated by nature, so tens or low hundreds of rows is the expected size; binding a raw transaction table will be slow and the chart will be unreadable.

property.caption: Columns
property.description: Used when Data from is Data source. Maps each attribute onto the key the chart expects, so no JSON is written anywhere. A Pie needs id and value; a Bar needs the index key plus one key per series; a point chart needs x and y. See nivo.rocks for the keys a given chart type reads. Attributes that are not mapped are simply left out of the datum.

property.caption: Attribute
property.description: The attribute to read from each row.

property.caption: Chart key
property.description: The key this attribute becomes in the chart datum — id, value, x, y, or a series name. Leave it empty to use the attribute's own name, which is convenient when the domain model already matches. Two columns writing the same key is reported rather than allowed: one would silently overwrite the other and the chart would draw with a column missing.

property.caption: Series
property.description: Used when Data from is Data source, and only by the chart types that draw several series — Line, Scatter Plot, Heat Map, Radial Bar, Bump and Area Bump. The rows are split on this attribute, and each distinct value becomes one series carrying its own points, in the order the data source returned them. Splitting is not aggregating: no row is combined with another, which is why it is allowed where summing is not. Leave it empty for every other chart type.

property.caption: Chart type
property.description: Which Nivo chart to render. Each chart type expects its own data shape and accepts its own configuration properties, so changing this usually means changing the bound data as well. This names the chart's form only; how it is drawn is the Renderer property below. Before 2.0 these keys carried a Responsive prefix and folded in the drawing technology; an expression written against 1.x needs updating.

property.caption: Chart type (dynamic)
property.description: Optional. An expression returning one of the chart type keys above, so the chart type can follow the data instead of being fixed when the page is built — a dashboard where the user picks a visualisation, or a chart whose form depends on the record. Where the key comes from a Mendix enumeration, getKey($currentObject/YourAttribute) returns it directly. When this is set and produces a recognised key it overrides Chart type; when it is empty the Chart type above is used. An unrecognised value is not silently ignored: the widget shows an error naming the value it was given, because a chart that quietly renders the wrong type is worse than one that says it cannot.

property.caption: Renderer
property.description: How the chart is drawn. SVG is the default and every chart type supports it. Canvas draws to a bitmap instead and is worth choosing where the element count is high enough that SVG becomes slow — large scatter plots, dense heat maps, long calendars. HTML exists for three hierarchical charts and lets their labels use ordinary text layout. Not every chart type has every renderer: fourteen have Canvas and three have HTML. Choosing one a chart type does not have is not an error — the chart is drawn as SVG instead, since the same chart is shown either way — but it is reported as a warning at design time so the choice is not silently doing nothing. Note the accessibility trade-off before choosing Canvas: SVG and HTML put every label in the DOM, where a screen reader and a browser text search can reach them, and Canvas puts none of them there — a Canvas chart is a single bitmap whose only accessible content is the Accessible label property. Prefer SVG unless the element count actually demands otherwise.

property.caption: Configuration (static)
property.description: Chart configuration as a JSON object, typed in here and fixed at design time. Use this for everything that does not change at runtime — axes, legends, margins, colour schemes. Merged first, so a value set here is overridden by the same key in the dynamic configuration or in a function property. Must be a valid JSON object; it is checked at design time.

property.caption: Configuration (dynamic)
property.description: String attribute holding chart configuration as a JSON object, so configuration can be built or changed at runtime — a colour scheme the user picks, a legend that depends on the data. Optional: leave it unbound if all configuration is static. Merged after the static configuration, so it wins on any key set in both. The attribute must be Unlimited length for the same reason the chart data must be. Note that more is expressible here than it first appears: a d3-format string for valueFormat or an axis format, and {"scheme":"nivo"} or {"datum":"data.color"} for colour, all avoid needing a function property. Where a value must be read off each datum, use a named function marker: "@fn:prop:size" reads the size field, "@fn:prop:data.color" walks a path, and "@fn:truncate:20" shortens a long label. Markers resolve by name against a fixed set the widget ships, so they need no 'unsafe-eval' and, unlike function properties, they work at runtime. A configuration value that names a FIELD BARE is the one thing to be wary of — Nivo 0.99 removed that form, so "nodeSize":"size" is read as a value rather than an accessor and renders nothing while reporting nothing. "@fn:prop:size" is what it should now say.

property.caption: Configuration (functions)
property.description: The last resort, for the few Nivo properties that need a function no other route can supply. TRY THE OTHER TWO FIRST, both of which work at runtime through the dynamic configuration and carry none of the costs below. ONE: most formatting is already declarative in Nivo 0.99 — valueFormat and axis format take a d3-format string such as ".1%", "~s" or "%b %Y", and colour takes {"scheme":"nivo"}, an explicit palette array, or {"datum":"data.color"}. TWO: to read a value off each datum, use a named function marker in the configuration — "nodeSize": "@fn:prop:size" is the runtime-safe replacement for the "nodeSize": "size" field-name form that Nivo 0.99 removed, and "@fn:truncate:20" shortens a long label. Only when neither fits — a tooltip whose content is computed, say — write a body here. Merged last, so a function property wins over both a marker and a JSON value on the same key. The costs, and they are why this is last: the bodies are not type-checked, they run with whatever Nivo passes them, they cannot be set at runtime at all because this is a design-time list, and compiling them needs 'unsafe-eval' in the page's Content-Security-Policy.

property.caption: Property name
property.description: The Nivo configuration property this function is assigned to, e.g. tooltip, valueFormat, colors. Spelling is not validated — a name Nivo does not recognise is silently ignored by the chart.

property.caption: Arguments
property.description: Comma-separated argument names for the function, matching what Nivo passes for this property — often a single argument such as datum or value. Leave empty for a function that takes none.

property.caption: Body
property.description: The function body, without the surrounding function declaration or braces. It must return a value: a body that falls off the end returns undefined, which Nivo usually renders as an empty tooltip or a missing label rather than an error. Syntax is checked at design time.

property.caption: Height mode
property.description: How the chart's height is decided. Nivo charts fill their container, so the container must have a height from somewhere — a chart in a container of zero height renders nothing at all, with no error.

property.caption: Height (px)
property.description: Chart height in pixels. Used only when Height mode is Fixed pixels; ignored otherwise.

property.caption: Aspect ratio
property.description: Width divided by height — 1.6 is roughly 16:10, 1 is square. The chart takes its width from the page and derives its height from this. Used only when Height mode is Aspect ratio; ignored otherwise.

property.caption: Empty message
property.description: Shown instead of the chart when the bound data is an empty array. Without it several chart types render an empty axis frame that looks like a broken chart rather than an absence of data, and a few throw. Leave empty to use the default text.

property.caption: Accessible label
property.description: Describes what the chart shows, for screen readers. A chart is an image to assistive technology: without this it is announced as nothing at all. Say what is being measured and over what, e.g. "Claims volume by month, split by peril" — not "bar chart".
